Aardvarks Can Smell Insects Buried Over a Meter Underground
Aardvarks hunt in near-total darkness. They don’t rely on sight at all. Instead, they follow an invisible trail beneath their feet.

Aardvarks have an extraordinarily powerful sense of smell that allows them to detect ants and termites buried more than a meter underground. Their long snouts house highly developed olfactory structures specialized for scent tracking. While foraging, an aardvark slowly moves across the ground, sniffing constantly. Once it detects a colony, it begins digging with precision. This ability lets aardvarks locate food sources that are completely hidden from other predators. It also reduces competition, since few animals can access these insects so efficiently.
This matters because it makes aardvarks highly specialized insect predators. Their success depends on sensory ability rather than speed or strength.
It also explains why aardvarks struggle when habitats are altered. Disrupting soil and insect populations removes their primary food signals.
Aardvarks can identify whether a termite mound is active or abandoned purely by smell. They rarely waste energy digging into empty nests.

Aardvarks Have Teeth With No Enamel
Aardvark teeth are unlike almost any other mammal’s. They don’t shine or sharpen the way you’d expect. In fact, they break most dental rules.

Aardvark teeth lack enamel entirely and are instead made of thousands of thin tubules of dentine. These tubules run vertically through the tooth, making it flexible and resistant to wear. Because aardvarks eat insects rather than chewing tough material, enamel isn’t necessary. Their teeth also grow continuously, compensating for constant abrasion. This unusual structure is unique among living mammals.
It matters because tooth structure reveals diet and evolution. Aardvarks adapted perfectly to their narrow feeding niche.
This uniqueness also helps scientists identify aardvark fossils. Their teeth are instantly recognizable in the fossil record.
If an aardvark loses part of a tooth, it doesn’t suffer the same way other mammals would. The tubule structure reduces cracking and damage.

Aardvarks Are the Only Living Members of Their Entire Order
Aardvarks have no close cousins walking the Earth today. They stand completely alone on the evolutionary tree. Their family reunion would be very quiet.

Aardvarks are the sole surviving species in the order Tubulidentata. All other members of this group went extinct millions of years ago. Despite superficial similarities to anteaters or pigs, aardvarks are not closely related to either. Genetic evidence places them in a distinct African lineage. This makes aardvarks evolutionary outliers.
It matters because losing aardvarks would mean losing an entire branch of mammalian history. No replacement species exists.
This uniqueness increases their conservation value. Protecting aardvarks preserves irreplaceable genetic diversity.
Their closest living relatives are actually elephants and manatees, not insect-eaters. This surprises many scientists.
